Anytype publishes a machine-readable OpenAPI document at developers.anytype.io/openapi-v2.yaml: info "title: Anytype API", "version: \"2025-11-08\"", with full component schemas and documented error responses ("Unauthorized ... Missing, unknown, revoked or expired key"). The spec file lives in the anyproto/anytype-api developer-portal repo as openapi-v2.yaml, synced from the anytype-heart core and published at /openapi-v2.yaml on releases.

The API reference is versioned with dated releases: "API Version: 2025-11-08", a version picker listing "API v2 — pre-release" alongside "API v1" versions "2025-11-08 (latest)", "2025-05-20", "2025-04-22", and a Changelog section. Portal banner: "Pre-release: Anytype API v2 is now available to try - objects as editable JSON documents, built for agents and humans." No written deprecation policy page and no try-it console are published.

The iOS version is very well-crafted, but the type on iPad Mini is much, much too small, even for someone who generally prefers small type.
Has used it for about a year as a very basic note system. Says it's very polished and has been stable, and the Apple and Android apps work well too.

Has followed Anytype since 2019. It went from a libp2p-based Google Docs alternative to something more complicated, with relations and sets. They never use it because it's too complicated (and Electron). Every time they open it they end up rewatching explainer videos. It gets in the way of doing things.

After trying dozens of note apps (Notion, Standard Notes, Joplin, Notesnook, Obsidian), finds Anytype 'at least barely acceptable'. It syncs notes between devices, works offline, is cross-platform, and has a decent editor with code highlighting. Weak points: the UX isn't nice yet, and the graph view is useless once you have hundreds of objects.

Questions why an offline app requires login and shows remote storage already in use. There's no option to set the local storage path, and saved files are opaque Electron blob files, so there's no way to access or control your files externally. Doesn't feel trustworthy.
Daily Notion user says Anytype looks full-featured and could easily replace Notion for them. The lack of a web app is what keeps them from switching, because it isn't portable enough for their work.
Points out the license on the anytype-ts GitHub repo isn't actually open source by the Open Source Definition, despite the open-source framing.

Was on the waitlist for about 5 years without ever getting an email. After installing, it looks nice but is too similar to Notion. They'll stick with Obsidian for its flexibility (running their own code, customizing everything).

Importing from Logseq or Obsidian is painful: one .md file at a time, and the zip option is confusing. It pushes you to organize up front. It's an awesome OneNote replacement and easy personal wiki, and P2P sync works fine. But the data format isn't findable; the local folder is a standard Electron folder, unusable for their own backups.
Heavy Notion user who has used Anytype for a while calls it a very nice, well-developed product. Glad it now has a mobile app, and sees it as a better, more secure alternative to Notion.

Compared to Obsidian, you can't use raw Markdown or CSV files with Anytype. They paid Obsidian $300+ for data independence and would want the same freedom with open-standard files from a local Notion alternative.

Uses it heavily. Some of it isn't intuitive coming from Notion, but the docs got them up to speed quickly. It feels joyful like Notion without the weight of Notion's features. There are some quality-of-life annoyances; they'd like alternate card previews and options to organize disconnected graphs.
Tried it about a year earlier. There was an hour-long onboarding session over Zoom before getting the download link, and the tool was too complicated. Moved to Zotero and plain-text files instead.

Outliner user wishes each block could behave like an object, the way tasks do. Converting blocks to objects is possible but defeats the outliner's bird's-eye view. They also need a merge feature so re-imported CSVs update existing database objects and keep their IDs and links.
Says what sets Anytype apart among local-first apps is its Notion-style databases, which they believe are unique in that space.

Creator of Turtl tried Anytype as a replacement. Complaints: the license is source-available, sharing isn't available yet despite being promoted, and data sits unencrypted on disk (encrypted in transit, not at rest). Still found the interface and utility amazing, 'like Notion mixed with a personal database', and sync between devices worked great.
Downloaded the alpha from download.anytype.io and it didn't work at all on their Mac, showing just a blank window.
Applied for an invite more than 2 years earlier and never received anything, even after emailing them.
Applied a year or two ago and kept getting onboarding invitations scheduled at times like Saturday 2am or Tuesday 8am PST, which they couldn't attend.
The slow, messy scrolling on the landing page is enraging on mobile, and seeing manifestos instead of a demo is a red flag.
